practice1.hint: There is no network here, so this exercise reads your code rather than running it. What it looks for is the three parts every real request has: the call, the check on what came back, and the parse.

questions.prompt: Which status code means the request succeeded?
questions.explain: 200 is OK. The 400s are problems with the request you sent, the 500s are problems on the server.

choices: The raw reply as one long string
A Python dictionary or list built from the JSON body
questions.explain: It parses the body for you. response.text is the same reply left as a string, which you would then have to hand to json.loads yourself.

questions.prompt: Match each status code to what it means.
right: The server broke while handling it
questions.explain: The code tells you whose problem it is, which decides whether retrying could ever help.

questions.prompt: Put the four steps of an API call in order.
items: Your program sends an HTTP request to the endpoint
The server processes the request and gathers the data
The server sends back a status code and a JSON body
Your program parses the JSON and uses the data
questions.explain: Nothing can be parsed before it has arrived, and nothing arrives before it is asked for. Each step waits on the one before it.

questions.prompt: Which of these make an API call safer to run unattended?
choices: Passing a timeout so the call cannot hang forever
Checking the status code, or calling raise_for_status()
Calling the API more often so a failure matters less
questions.explain: A timeout bounds the wait, the status check bounds what you trust, and the except bounds the damage. Calling more often just fails more often.

reflection-exercise1.hint: Describe the round trip: what you send, what comes back, and what you have to do to the reply before you can use it.

reflection-exercise2.hint: Say what a GET asks the server to do, and name the code that says it worked.
